Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture. Has the minister anything further to report in respect to the very

disastrous crop conditions in western Canada and, in particular, can the minister inform the house whether the government has in mind any action for making direct payments to producers who suffer crop losses or losses in income?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CROP CONDITIONS IN WESTERN CANADA

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CROP CONDITIONS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia was away on one type of business while I was away in respect to the business of the western farmers.
A meeting of the three western agriculture ministers and their staffs, the premier of Manitoba, the Minister of National Defence and myself representing the federal government, was held last Sunday in Winnipeg. At that time we went over the plans of the various provinces to meet the exceptional drought conditions of this year in the west. We formally went through the plans for the traditional freight assistance for the movement of fodder to cattle. It was made clearly apparent that in many parts of the country there would not be enough fodder to move even if there was freight assistance, so we discussed a program of switching the farmers in western Canada who have cattle herds to feeding grain in preference to fodder.
The federal government also made an offer to the provinces to double its community pasture program whereby the federal government would move grain to the community pastures enabling the doubling of the population if necessary, so that farmers not able to get fodder and who do not have water could bring their cattle to these pastures. The provincial and federal governments agreed that there should be a joint program of extension aimed particularly at the agricultural population of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, to point out the economics of grain feeding as opposed to fodder feeding and how the techniques of switching from one grain to another which is in supply can be used.
We discussed at some length the application of the agricultural prices support legislation, but it was the hope of us all that by certain techniques we could keep the flow of cattle moving to commercial markets in
Inquiries of the Ministry such a way that prices would not drop, so there would be no need to use price supports. The provincial governments expressed gratification in respect to our willingness to use support prices, and we discussed various grades to which it would apply, and so on.
Finally I should like to add a word and say that the situation as far as the cattle industry is concerned is quite serious. Weather conditions have deteriorated during the last 10 days. However, the essential fact to keep in mind is that there is no surplus of beef production in North America. There is no need for prices to decline if the movement of cattle to market is kept under good control. It was the declared intention of the four governments to see that this is done.
In regard to the last question asked by the hon. member in relation to payments, I think I can say that the federal government in 1958, through the words of the Prime Minister and his national agricultural program, among other things offered a program of crop insurance and a program of forage banks. I think the events of the last few months indicate the wisdom of this program, and I am sure the experience this year will convince the provincial governments across Canada that they would be very wise to inaugurate a hard sell campaign, selling crop insurance to farmers to enable farmers to build up a fund to meet this type of emergency, so as not to be faced with the tremendous drop in income such as they are now faced with.
The federal government stands ready at all times to see that everything possible is done to ameliorate conditions in any part of Canada, whether it be Prince Edward Island or the western provinces.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. Does the minister not feel that consideration should be given to cash payments to western producers, not only because of crop losses but also because of the added expense this year of combating the grasshopper and cutworm plagues? My second supplementary question, in view of the minister's reference to crop insurance, is this. I wonder whether the government has under consideration any amendments to the act so the federal government itself might bear part of the liability for crop losses, the whole of which is now shouldered by provincial governments; and has the government considered any change in its 20 per cent payment toward premium costs?

I should like to answer the second part of the question first. The present Crop Insurance Act is enabling

Inquiries of the Ministry legislation which allows any province to set up a scheme suitable to its own needs. The federal government provides 20 per cent of the premium by way of assistance to farmers to induce them to participate. There is nothing to prevent any provincial government from joining with the federal government in giving help by way of a contribution to the farmer's premium.
Second, the government is considering ways and means to improve any and all of our legislation, and this includes the crop insurance legislation. I think it is very clear that if under the terms of the present act there is overpayment on any insurance scheme in the first few years after the insurance plan has been set up there will be a heavy burden, but the fact remains that the federal government has offered to lend such schemes 75 per cent of the cost of any over-call on the scheme.
There has been a suggestion by the province of Manitoba that there be an additional reinsurance provision so that any province would not be seriously jeopardized in its credit arrangements if there was a heavy loss. This particular aspect of the situation is under review.
With regard to the first part of the hon. member's question as to the general loss suffered by farmers, I think this government has demonstrated that whenever there has been a serious loss of income, as in the case of the farmers of Prince Edward Island last fall with regard to their potatoes and as in the case of the western farmers, we have always been ready to consider some suitable means of coming to their assistance. I should like to remind the house that in 1958 and in 1960 the federal government made an acreage payment to western farmers which was opposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and now I have-

Inquiries of the Ministry for stretching out the work at the Florence colliery and, if so, what attitude had been taken by the company.
I am informed that a meeting was held on Friday, June 23, between representatives of the united mine workers and of the government on the closure of this colliery. At this meeting a proposal was made that some amount of additional work could be made available if complete salvage was made of all the equipment in the mine. It was agreed to refer this proposal to the company for its consideration and advice with the understanding that, if found practical by the company, the government would consider some financial assistance to permit of full recovery.
The proposal was placed before the president of Dominion Steel and Coal Company, and the technical details were also reviewed with the vice president in charge of mining operations. The government did not make any proposal, but simply transmitted to the company for consideration and advice the suggestion made at the meeting. The company advised that, both on general and technical grounds, the complete salvage of all material was not practical, and that the amount of extra employment that might be made available was not sufficient to justify the effort.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Laurier asked the following question:
Has the Canadian government authorized the installation by the United States of an atomic powered weather station in the Canadian Arctic?
The answer is that as part of a continuing program of meteorological research in the Arctic, the meteorological branch of the Department of Transport and the United States weather bureau arranged earlier this year for the installation and testing of a new automatic weather reporting device designed in the United States. The electrical energy required to power the device will come not from an atomic reactor but from radioactive isotopes. Heat generated by these isotopes will be converted into electrical power by means of a thermocouple. Plans call for the equipment to be installed on Graham island in the Queen Elizabeth islands, and the information it transmits will be picked up by the weather station at Resolute Bay.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF EXCHANGE SECTION BEFORE PRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is no. Of course it is no. To talk about this as being a leak is just unadulterated nonsense. I made it

quite clear in reply to a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam that Mr. Rasminsky, who is the Canadian representative on the executive board of the international monetary fund, was authorized by me to indicate confidentially and in only general terms to Mr. Per Jacobsson, the managing director of the international monetary fund, the general nature of the proposal that was to be made in the budget of June 20 in relation to the external value of the Canadian dollar.
It will be remembered that this was a statement of policy on the part of the government, not a statement on a particular measure. That was all that Mr. Jacobsson was made acquainted with in the conversation that Mr. Rasminsky had with Mr. Jacobsson in Washington on Tuesday, June 20. The following morning, as I also said yesterday, Mr. Rasminsky met with his fellow directors of the executive board of the international monetary fund and discussed with them the budget which had then been released and of which copies were then available in Washington; but Mr. Rasminsky until then was not acquainted with the budget. I pointed out last night that he was acquainted with only two chapters in the budget in general terms because of the fact that he is the manager of our exchange fund. This was just a normal consultation in regard to the management of the fund.
Therefore Mr. Speaker, to attempt to picture this as a budget leak is, I say, a travesty of the facts. I point out also, as I did yesterday, that in relation to the value established for the Canadian dollar in accordance with the article of the international monetary fund, on two occasions-

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF EXCHANGE SECTION BEFORE PRESENTATION

Governor of Bank of Canada

speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Last evening we on this side of the chamber did our best to get at some of the reasons underlying this bill of attainder and some explanation for the star chamber procedures which are embodied in it. That was not very easy because the minister, who gives us whatever information he sees fit, has said we are not entitled, in this court of appeal, on this issue, where the truth is not being heard, to what he considers to be confidential information. So we are restricted to what statements he sees fit to make on the various questions that we put to him in connection with a bill that is of such fundamental importance because it involves basic elements of decency, justice and fair play.
Perhaps the most important element in the consideration of this bill in committee is the reason the minister has given for the introduction of the bill, namely the impossibility of securing co-operation from the man whom

Governor of Bank of Canada the bill is designed to fire. The minister made an extraordinary statement last evening, among other extraordinary statements, when he said it was impossible to get that kind of co-operation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: What page?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Page 7521 of Hansard. They did not really try, out of respect for the sincerity of Mr. Coyne. It was quite out of keeping to ask him to put aside his views and co-operate, so they decided instead, out of respect for his sincerity, to demand that he put aside his job.
The one concrete charge levelled in this field of non co-operation, which was contradicted by the minister himself at the time and subsequently but it is still persisted in by the minister and it was repeated at page 7040 of Hansard, is this:
In the winter of 1957-58 I conveyed to him-
That is the governor:
-a request for an easing of the requirements respecting the liquidity reserves of chartered banks. That request, which was designed by the government to ease tight money, was rejected by the governor firmly and angrily.
There was certainly no indication at the time that the minister took anything but a favourable view of the policy of the bank. However, we dealt with that point last night and I do not intend to repeat it. I would like to ask the minister certain questions arising out of the statement he has made.
The minister said that this request was made-and it is a very important one, because on this request hangs the government's case-in the winter of 1957-58. I would like to ask the minister precisely when this request was made, not "in the winter of 195758". When was it made? Under what circumstances was it made? What were the details of the request made by the government of the governor in this field of monetary policy, for which at that time the government said they had no responsibility?
I would like to ask the minister what reason was given by the governor at that time for, as he puts it, rejecting this particular request. I would like to ask the minister whether he took any further action or made any further request of the governor or any servant of the bank, or any of the banks, respecting this particular matter at that particular time. If so, with what results?
I ask these specific questions of the minister in the light of the statement made on June 15 by the governor of the Bank of Canada when he said:
I repeat again that at no time has the Minister of Finance criticized or expressed a difference of opinion with the monetary policy being pursued


by the Bank of Canada which the bank and its board of directors were entitled to assume carried the tacit approval of the government.
Now the minister has told us there was one time-and he does not give us details of the time, place or circumstances-away back in the winter of 1957-58 when the governor angrily and firmly refused such a request. Now we should like to have information about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: I supplied information last night with regard to that occasion. I said it occurred in my office in this building, and I referred to those who were present, other officials of the Bank of Canada as well as the deputy minister of finance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: What date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
I shall not attempt to fix the date precisely. The occasion was, I would say, very late in 1957. It would be November or December of 1957, and the occasion was one on which I conveyed to the governor a request of the government for a reduction in the liquidity reserve requirements with reference to the chartered banks, which then was 15 per cent, having been advanced to that figure at the time of the imposition of the tight money policy a year and a half earlier.
I have said that this was a definite proposal and a definite request, and it was rejected. It was rejected at the time. The governor said he did not consider it sound that there should be any reduction in the prevailing 15 per cent requirement. He rejected the proposal firmly. As I said last night, he rejected it firmly, flatly and angrily. That made it clear that the governor felt himself under no obligation to give effect to requests of the government with respect to monetary action, because this was a definite request which had obvious and immediate implications for monetary policy.
From that point on, as I have said, the governor having taken that position, I turned to examine precisely my authority in this situation, and I found that under the existing statute I had been given by parliament no express authority to issue directives to the governor of the Bank of Canada in relation to such questions. I found also that the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act are perfectly clear in vesting in the bank the right and authority to create money. There is no authority reserved to the government in that regard.
That has been basic in the relations between the government and the governor from that time to this. I have said that the authorities of the bank-it was not the governor only-were always prepared to indicate what steps they were taking in the monetary field

or to defend what they were doing; but as to the authority, it had been clearly established right from the beginning that the government had no authority over the Bank of Canada in relation to such matters.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Well, the minister has not dealt with my question. He has dealt with some things which I did not raise, though they are very interesting. He has indicated, for instance-and this is of some importance in the light of certain disclosures last evening -that he was not sure of his authority in this field, apparently, until this particular incident took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: No. This is what I said. In line with what I had said while in opposition, I thought there was some authority possessed by the government in this field. I was brought up very short at that meeting. That led me to examine the statute and to conclude that no authority had been given to the government in this field to give directives to the bank.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Well, until this incident the minister had thought he had some authority in this field. It was not very long before this meeting that he was very clear and certain about the authority of the government in this sphere. When this meeting took place he was of the opinion that he might have some authority, but then he discovered he had no authority or responsibility in the field of monetary policy, at least until last evening.
May I ask the minister whether this clash- and we certainly have the right to call it a clash in view of the terms the minister has used, because this was a request which was firmly and angrily rejected by the governor- took place before or after November 13, 1957? Hon. members may recall that on November 13, 1957 the minister, replying to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano as reported on page 1063 of Hansard, said he was not aware of anything that could be called a clash between the government and the bank.
I should like also to ask the minister, while we are on this basic incident whether a record of any kind was made of this meeting, the conclusions of which were so important in the minds of the government that three and a half years later, based largely on those conclusions, they decided to introduce an act of parliament to discharge the governor of the Bank of Canada without giving him the right to be heard. This obviously was an important meeting. This is the incident upon which the government builds up its accusation. It was years ago, but it is on this basis that the government decided that the governor had to go. As I say, this was obviously a very important meeting because of the important and responsible people who
Governor of Bank of Canada attended it, and I ask if any record was made of this meeting, which the minister thinks may have taken place in December, 1957; whether there is anything which he could disclose from such a record.
I should also like the minister to deal with the other question I have asked him. I should like the hon. gentleman to tell us whether any further requests of this nature were made of the governor or of any servant of the bank, or of any of the banks; and if so, what was the result of any such request which was made subsequent to this meeting which took place some time in the autumn, presumably in December of 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
I am not sure that I followed all the points raised by the Leader of the Opposition, but if I overlook anything perhaps he will draw it to my attention. No communication in writing passed between the governor and myself in relation to this incident. Any communication of such a nature would, of course, have been confidential. I have drawn attention to this matter because it established very clearly the fact that the governor held a different view from the one I had entertained and had expressed while in opposition as to the relationship of the government to monetary policy.
It was made quite clear that the governor made the decisions in relation to action in the monetary field and considered himself under no obligation whatever to accept directives from the government. It was a precise proposal which I put before him, and I did so on behalf of the government. It was not something that I put to him on my own account. It was something which was conveyed to him-and he was so informed-coming from the government. He rejected it. It was perfectly clear that in the view of the governor he was under no obligation whatever in the sphere of monetary action to accept directives from the government. As I say, this proposal which the government put forward was rejected flatly and angrily.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Does the minister not agree that the liquidity requirement, and that is what we are talking about, was not approved by the governor but was accepted voluntarily by the chartered banks on the suggestion of the government? Does the minister not recall that in the Bank of Canada report of 1955 there was included the statement that the function of a minimum liquid asset ratio is to increase the effectiveness of monetary policy in moderating a too rapid expansion of credit? A little further on, at page 16 of this report, appears the following statement:
Alter discussion, the banks have agreed to work to achieve by May 31, 1956 a minimum liquid asset

Governor of Bank of Canada ratio of 15 per cent which they will endeavour to maintain on a daily average basis from June on.
Is the minister really trying to tell this committee that on the basis of this one meeting, in respect to matters about which the minister is so vague that he doesn't even know when it was held and has no record of it, but suggests it was in 1957, sometime in September, the government in 1961 has decided to introduce a bill to discharge the governor of the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition would perhaps be closer to accuracy and orderly procedure if he would stick to his questions instead of jumping to conclusions, because the conclusions are so definitely wrong. He does not wait for an answer to get the facts but jumps at conclusions and consequently makes statements which are quite at variance with the facts.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: If he waits for an answer he will grow old in the process.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Chairman, may we proceed with the answers to the questions? The Leader of the Opposition, it was quite obvious as soon as he started, has obtained and accepted in full Mr. Coyne's version of the increase, at the time of the application of the tight money policy, a year and a half before we came into office, in the liquid reserves of chartered banks from 8 per cent to 15 per cent. Mr. Coyne, in the report which the Leader of the Opposition read and on other occasions, has taken the ground that this was agreed to or undertaken voluntarily by the chartered banks.
I have to say that this is a matter of the clearest kind of dispute between Mr. Coyne's version of what happened and the version of the chartered banks, because I had occasion in those days to confer with a number of the chartered banks on this question, and the answers I invariably received from them were that this was imposed upon them by Mr. Coyne and they did not agree to it. They firmly disagreed with the statement which appeared in the report of the governor of the bank which the Leader of the Opposition has read. That is the fact, and that is the difference in the statement in that regard which is wide and complete.
It will be remembered also by hon. members that when the tight money policy was instituted a year and a half before we came into office, this increase from 8 per cent to 15 per cent in the liquid reserves requirement of the chartered banks obliged the chartered banks to market, at a time when the market was not strong, vast holdings of Dominion of Canada bonds, and that the

chartered banks in the course of that enforced liquidation sustained very heavy losses. This was a matter, therefore, that the banks regarded as of some considerable importance. They have not forgotten that on that occasion, as they have made very clear, a policy was imposed by the governor of the Bank of Canada which obliged them to liquidate their substantial holdings, running into hundreds of millions of dollars in dominion government bonds, with consequent very heavy losses. From that time on the chartered banks have naturally been much more cautious in their lending policies, because they had no assurance that there would not be a repetition of what had happened to them in that unhappy experience of 1955-56.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when answering a question the Minister of Finance roams all over. What did I ask the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I did so because the chartered banks-

speechtext: Please answer the question very simply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: -considered in this respect, quite at variance with the statement of Mr. Coyne, that a requirement had been imposed upon them to increase from 8 per cent to 15 per cent, and hold at 15 per cent, their liquid reserves.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: What statutory authority was there for that?

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 should like to continue the matter referred to by the Leader of the Opposition. It seems to me we are seeking a break-through in the wall, although I do not think we are getting very far. Last night I listened to the remarks of the Minister of Finance, and his words had a very familiar ring. I went back to my office and looked up his former words, and

found that he was using exactly the same phrases and words as before, just as though it was a replay of the same record. There is no new information forthcoming, and I suggest this is becoming an exercise in futility. I suggest the reason for this is that whenever the Leader of the Opposition seeks to ferret out information the answer is given that the information is confidential. I suggest that the minister is being very selective in regard to what he determines is confidential.
Last night the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked for particular advice which the governor had given to the Minister of Finance in respect to debt management in relation to the present budget. I suggest this is an extremely important matter, because the minister has stated in this house that the reason the governor of the Bank of Canada must go is that the expansion budget which has been presented is opposed by the governor and, therefore, he must be relieved of his duties in order that this expansion budget may be brought to a successful conclusion. The main reason given for his having to go is his lack of co-operation with this expansionist government.
We have no way of finding out what the governor of the Bank of Canada advised in relation to this budget because the Minister of Finance refuses to give the information on the ground that it is confidential. As an example of that, when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked for information, the Minister of Finance said the following, as reported at page 7520 of Hansard of July 4, 1961:
That hon. member asked me specifically to disclose the advice given by Mr. Coyne to the government in relation to certain questions of debt management with respect to the money-raising program for the present year. It would he highly improper on my part to disclose advice given to me or to the government by the adviser in this respect,-
Then he went on to say the following:
It would be very unfair either to the adviser in this particular case or the advisers of the government in other cases if ministers were to disclose in the house advice of a very confidential nature given to them in this regard.
When it was suggested that the information was being hidden the minister then said the following, as reported on the same date:
-it remains hidden for very good reasons of public policy. It has always been so under our system of government.
I should like to point out that although this information is considered confidential, the advice given by the governor of the Bank of Canada in 1957-58 apparently was not confidential, because the Minister of Finance has brought that information to the attention of this house. The minister stated that the 90205-6-477
Governor of Bank of Canada governor refused to accept certain proposals by the government, angrily and completely, which apparently brought the Minister of Finance up very short because he went into very great detail, as reported at page 7524 of Hansard of July 4, 1961, to describe what took place at this meeting held in his office in this building, which would appear to be a regular meeting and which would be confidential. I think the minister is being rather selective in considering what is confidential and what is not confidential.
The Leader of the Opposition this morning has presented the one shred of evidence of a real difference between the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada which has given rise, four years later, to a desire for his resignation. I should very much like to know why the advice given by the governor of the Bank of Canada in 1957-58, which was revealed by the Minister of Finance, not by the governor of the bank, was not considered to be confidential.
In all the letters of the governor of the Bank of Canada he has stated that there has been complete co-operation without any area of disagreement. He has also stated he was willing to co-operate in regard to the present budget, and that he has desired to co-operate all down the line. Why is it, I ask the Minister of Finance, that the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada in 1961 is confidential but was not confidential back in 1957 and 1958?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

The hon. member has not appreciated the difference in what is involved here. I was asked last night to disclose advice received from the governor of the Bank of Canada in relation to a matter of debt management and I declined to give that information. In that realm the Bank of Canada acts as adviser to the government. The government takes full responsibility for the decisions, and it would be highly improper under such circumstances to disclose the advice received.
The incident which has been discussed here this morning was not a matter of advice on the part of the governor at all. The whole point is that this was the field in which he made decisions. I referred to the fact that a particular request had been made by the government and a decision had been taken by the governor. There is a great difference between advice in the one case and a decision in the other, and it is the decision that I have given to the house.

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
Would the conversation that took place at that particular meeting in 195758 not be regarded as confidential by those who attended the meeting?

Governor of Bank of Canada

subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

This is fundamental to what has happened since, and it is fundamental to all this discussion that has gone on at this stage and earlier stages of this matter. The governor gave the answer that I have related to the house. It was a decision; it was an act, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: May I ask the minister if this was the first fundamental difference that took place between the government on one hand and the governor on the other hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: I would say yes. This was quite fundamental, Mr. Chairman. It certainly rocked me to find that this request from the government was firmly rejected, and angrily rejected.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext: What did the minister do in the face of this attitude taken by the governor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR
speechtext:
There was nothing I could do. As I have said, I went to the statute to see if I had the authority that previously I had assumed that the government had, which was the basis of the view I had expressed in the house when in opposition, particularly in the debate of 1956, and I found there no express authority given to the government to give directives to the governor of the Bank of Canada.
It is a fact, Mr. Chairman, that in this respect the Bank of Canada Act does not follow the terms of the Bank of England act. Under an amendment to the Bank of England act made in 1945, I think it was, express authority is given to the treasury, which means to the chancellor of the exchequer, to give directives to the governor of the Bank of England, but there is no such authority given to the government under our Bank of Canada Act, or given to the Minister of Finance in relation to the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CREATION OF VACANCY IN OFFICE OF GOVERNOR

The subcommittee of the board which considered this question, according to the record and according to my information, was composed of three members, two drawn from appointees of the present government and one appointee of the former government. As I have said, my information is that the by-law, including the special provision made for the pensions of the governor and deputy governor, was approved unanimously. writer of that article keeps going back again and again to assert that the prime reason for asking for the resignation of the governor was this matter of the pension. This was one of five reasons. The article takes us back to the first statement issued by the governor, who gave a very misleading impression of the conference held on May 30. I wish to deal particularly with what that erroneous and misleading article says with regard to the pension. This article seems to suggest that this pension is comparable with those payable in the civil service. I say that is a very misleading presentation.
The superannuation act was amended at the 1960 session of parliament on motion of the government and the effect of that amendment was to increase the superannuation provisions so that persons qualifying under the act might have a pension based on 35 years' contribution at the rate of 2 per cent per annum and with the pension based upon the six best earning years. The highest salary paid in the civil service, as was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Carleton is $24,000 a year. That is the highest salary paid. How anybody can make 70 per cent of that come anywhere near the pension payable to the governor will be a stretching of any mathematical process.
But that tells only a small part of the story. The fact is that these pensions under the superannuation act are payable to persons retiring at age 65. Here is the governor who is able to retire at age 51 and draw a pension of $25,000 per annum. Moreover, the pension payable under the superannuation act is a contributory pension and the rate of contributions was increased last year. But what about this pension, this increase? It was a contributory pension, it is true, when on February 15, 1960, the board of directors of the bank increased it. Up till that time the contributions by the governor had been $1,500 per annum but when his pension rate was more than doubled on that occasion what about the contribution? He does not contribute on a full salary of $50,000 a year. Under the by-law he contributes on only $40,000 of that. I am informed that in 1960 his pension contributions, following the increase on February 15, amounted to a total of $2,287.50 of which $1,500, of course, was deductible from his income for tax purposes and $787.50 was taxable. This year, 1961, if his contributions run a full year, he will contribute $2,400, of which $1,500 will be deductible from income for tax purposes and $900 will be taxable.
Now, Mr. Chairman, when I look around the civil service of this country and I see a writer in the Ottawa Citizen comparing the pension rights available to the governor under
Governor of Bank of Canada this pension by-law of February 15, 1960 and think of the provisions that are available to civil servants, then I say I do not know of any civil servant in this country who would not jump at the opportunity to trade places with the governor under those circumstances. As a matter of fact, I think most people in this country would jump at the opportunity to trade places with anyone who could retire at age 51 on a pension of $25,000 a year for life.

Governor of Bank of Canada he will forgo or waive the pension to which he is entitled from the bank; that is just made out of somebody's imagination,
I refer hon. members to what I said at page 7178 of Hansard of June 28. When he decided to give his personal advice to the governor of the Bank of Canada, did the minister, using his phrase reported at page 7040 of the House of Commons debates of June 26, 1961, "scurry again" to look at the Bank of Canada Act and find what his rights were? Did he scurry again, as a very able lawyer and a bright boy, to look at the evidence contained in the reports of the House of Commons committee on banking and commerce in 1954 when we together looked very carefully into the responsibilities assigned to the government and to the governor in these matters?
I regard the Minister of Finance as a bright boy, and have always held that opinion of him. However, inasmuch as the Minister of Finance was the chief spokesman for his party when in opposition at the time when the banking laws in this country were being reviewed in 1954 by the standing committee on banking and commerce-and the hon. gentleman's name appears on almost everyone of the 900 pages of the report of that committee -I find it difficult to understand how he can come to parliament in his ministerial office almost four years later and say that in 1957-58


he conveyed to the governor of the Bank of Canada a request for the easing up of the requirements respecting the liquidity reserves of the chartered banks. That statement can be found at page 7040 of Hansard for June 26, 1961, where he also says that, as a bright boy, he then scurried to read the Bank of Canada Act.
The minister had just participated in an election campaign at that time during which both he and the present Prime Minister, both eminent lawyers, had been screaming about the tight money policy. I cannot believe that those two hon. gentlemen were so irresponsible as to go to the Canadian electorate, as they did during the campaign that year, without having read carefully the responsibilities of the government vis-a-vis the governor of the Bank of Canada in connection with monetary policy. However, that is the explanation given by the minister during the current debate.
I suggest to the minister, and challenge him to correct me, that he has shown no inconsistency during any budget debate between his own statements and statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada. On the contrary, my belief is that only during recent weeks has the minister been defeated by his colleagues in the cabinet in respect to policies regarding which he has not differed from those espoused by the governor. I can refer to them if the minister wishes me to, because some other statements were made by him in the course of presenting his preliminary budget in 1959 to his friends in Toronto.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak on third reading of this bill for only a very few moments. I intend to put the issue, as we see it, before the house on this bill. It is a simple issue, but it is a fundamentally important issue and no smokescreen of any kind, no oratorical invective or exuberance should be allowed to obscure this issue. The issue, Mr. Speaker, is not that of the policy of the person or of the tactics of the governor of the Bank of Canada. The issue is not even whether the governor of the Bank of Canada has co-operated or not co-operated with the government in financial matters in which cooperation from him is desirable, indeed is essential and in some cases is required by law and is certainly required in practice. The governor says he has so co-operated. The minister says that he has not co-operated since at least, November, 1957. This is July, 1961.
But that is not the issue. The issue is one of simply the fundamental right of justice and fair play, the right of a Canadian to be heard before condemnation and to be heard before the body which is condemning him. It is a right enshrined in that clause of the bill of rights which says that no Canadian act of

Governor of Bank of Canada parliament-and we are dealing with a Canadian act of parliament-no Canadian order or rule or regulation or law, shall be construed or applied so as to deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations. By a "hearing" surely is not meant in that clause of the bill of rights the right, in default of a hearing before a court or tribunal, to write letters. So I ask the government this question: How dare it violate this right in this case or in any other case, a government which so often boasts about its devotion to this same bill of rights. In this controversy between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, this right is being denied if we pass this bill because we in this House of Commons by this bill shall have condemned the governor. We shall have thrown him out of his job by act of parliament without giving him an opportunity to state his case before the body which is being asked to take action. That is the issue, Mr. Speaker, and that is the only issue, namely such a right to be heard by or before a body which the Minister of Finance once called the high court of appeal; such a right to be heard in simple, elementary justice.
Oh, the hearing might have taken two or three days, if it had been permitted. It might have been inconvenient. It might have been embarrassing to the government or it might have been embarrassing to the governor. However, we would have had an opportunity in this House of Commons, through an agency of the house, to examine the evidence, to summon witnesses and to get as near to the facts of the case as was humanly possible; and on the basis of the evidence, and only that kind of evidence, would we then have been asked to take the action which is embodied in a bill.
I do not know what would have happened if that procedure had been followed. Surely the government by now must be sorry that they did not follow it. Naturally we on this side of the house are suspicious as a result of the refusal of the government to allow this matter to go to a committee. It flatly refuses to allow any evidence to appear in this House of Commons except that evidence which it wishes to bring forward or the evidence we can get on published documents by the governor of the bank and others.
I know this, Mr. Speaker, and the house must know it. Because we are not giving this hearing to the governor of the Bank of Canada, a high public official, we are violating his basic right to be heard before the tribunal which is being asked to condemn him, and to do so on the basis of evidence supplied in this house by the government

alone. When we produce evidence supplied in the press-and that is the only place to which he has access-the Minister of Finance says that it is not true, that it is distorted, that it is false or uses other words of that kind, a procedure which makes it difficult indeed for us to get to the facts of this situation in a way in which we could have done it if there had been a committee.
The fact that the governor, prevented for years from appearing before a commons committee, has circulated letters defending himself against charges which have now been made against him, or the fact that his tactics and some of his statements in his defence may be open to criticism, does not alter his right to be heard. We are the ones on this side who have criticized some of the policies and some of the tactics of the governor in the past, but we now support his right to defend himself against those who accuse him. The House of Commons is being asked to discharge the governor of the Bank of Canada, a public official, who will not resign voluntarily because he asserts that the charges made against him are wrong, that they do him a grave injustice, and that he is entitled to be heard by parliament in respect of those charges before parliament takes action against him. So I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that for the House of Commons to take the action recommended in this bill without the governor's being given the opportunity which he seeks to appear before a committee of this house would be an intolerable and indefensible violation of an elementary right of a free Canadian citizen. Because of that fact we will vote against third reading of this bill.

Then I began to search further. Of course we all know that the constitution of the United States was based in substance on the history, traditions, practices and procedures of the parliament of Great Britain. That was the foundation of the constitution. I read a book entitled "The Liberties of an American" written by Mr. Leo Pfeifer, a very well known advocate in the United States. On page 165 of this book, under a paragraph headed "Bills of attainder" we find the following:
Both the federal government and the states are forbidden by the constitution to enact bills of attainder. A bill of attainder is an act of the legislature inflicting punishment upon a person or persons who have not been convicted in a judicial trial. It needs little argument to show that punishment by legislative act without judicial trial does not accord with democratic concepts of fair play, besides being inconsistent with the American system of the separation of powers.
Historically bills of attainder concerned themselves only with punishment, but, as in the case of ex post facto laws, the supreme court held that a disqualification for an office or profession imposed upon individuals by act of the legislature may constitute punishment and thus be a bill of attainder.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I understand the reason why the hon. member for Essex East has constantly referred to this bill as a bill of attainder. subtopic: REPORT OF FIFTH MEETING OF CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The fifth meeting of the Canada-United States interparliamentary group was held in Washington and Norfolk, Virginia, from Wednesday, June 7, to Sunday, June 11, both inclusive. Twenty four members of the congress of the United States and 24 members of the parliament of Canada participated.
The group held two plenary sessions and two series of committee meetings on Thursday and Friday. One committee discussed defence and foreign policy, while the other committee discussed economic matters of interest to both countries. The first committee met under the co-chairmanship of Senator Homer Capehart, and later Senator George Aiken, and Speaker Mark Drouin. The second committee was co-chaired by Representative Cornelius Gallagher and Speaker Roland Michener.
The Canadian delegates were welcomed at the opening plenary session on Thursday, June 8, by Secretary of State, Dean Rusk, who underlined the importance of these meetings of legislators as a valuable means of promoting better understanding and appreciation of their mutual problems. Later that morning the Canadian delegates proceeded to the floor of the United States Senate and were welcomed by Senators Aiken, Mansfield, Dirksen, Capehart, Keating, Humphrey, Johnson, Javits, Allott, Fong and Senator Hickey, the presiding officer. The statements of welcome are printed in Appendix "B" of this report.
Representative Gallagher was host at a luncheon in the old supreme court chamber, an historic room of the Capitol building which served as the Senate chamber from 1819 to
1859	and as the supreme court chamber from
1860	to 1935. The wives of the delegates were entertained at luncheon by Mrs. Fulbright and Mrs. Gallagher. Following these luncheons the members of the Canadian delegation and their wives had the honour of being received by the President at the White house.
Later in the afternoon the co-chairmen participated in a ceremony at the zoological gardens of the Smithsonian institute, when a pair of Canadian beavers, the gift of the government of Canada, was formally presented to the director of the institute. The occasion was enlivened by the presence of a baby beaver born to the pair in Washington a few
days before. That evening the Canadian delegation and their wives were the guests at a dinner given by the United States delegation.
On Friday, following the conclusion of the business sessions, the Canadian delegates were the guests of Senator Aiken at a luncheon in the old supreme court chamber. Meanwhile the wives of the Canadian delegates enjoyed a very pleasant cruise on the Potomac river on board President Kennedy's yacht, the Honey Fitz. Members of both delegations and their wives left Washington late Friday afternoon for Norfolk, Virginia, where they were the guests of the continental army command for the week end. On Saturday, after the inspection of a guard of honour and the firing of a 19-gun salute, the delegates attended air and ground exercises at Fort Storey and Fort Eustis near Norfolk. The group also visited the national aeronautical space agency for a briefing on "project Mercury" by Mr. Carpenter, one of the seven United States astronauts, and other members of the agency. On the same day, the wives of the delegates visited Jamestown and Williamsburg for a tour of historic sights. Both delegations returned to their respective capitals on Sunday afternoon.
Committee Discussions
The discussions in the committees took place with the same spirit of frankness and respect for divergent views as has characterized discussions at previous meetings. The personnel of the two committees is shown in Appendix "A" of this report. At the closing plenary session on Friday, reports of the two committees were approved for inclusion in a press release. This press release was distributed at a press conference held by the four co-chairmen prior to the departure for Norfolk. The committee reports are reprinted in Appendix "C" of this report.
Conclusions
This latest meeting of the Canada-United States interparliamentary group confirmed once again the usefulness of such exchanges. All delegates, many of whom were attending for the first time, welcomed the opportunities given to them both in the business sessions and on informal occasions for discussions with their United States colleagues. The Canadian delegates wish to express their

warm appreciation for the cordial hospitality of President Kennedy, the members of the United States delegation, and the commanding general and officers of the United States continental army command.
As a result of the policy of including new personnel in the delegations for each meeting, 56 members of congress and seventy members of parliament have now taken part in one or more of the meetings held since January, 1959. As on previous occasions, the attendance of the wives of the delegates did much to confirm and strengthen in social exchange the friendships formed in the conferences themselves.
In submitting this report, we also wish to acknowledge the co-operation and express our appreciation for the assistance of officials of the various departments of the Canadian government who helped with the arrangements for the meeting.
Mark R. Drouin Roland Michener Speaker of the Senate Speaker of the House
of Commons Joint Chairmen Dated at Ottawa July 5, 1961.

speechtext: Mr. President, I wish to join the distinguished senator from Vermont, who has led the Senate group so ably in our discussions with our Canadian colleagues for the past several years. speechtext:
Mr. President, in a world that is so full of ugly fevers and contagion today, we can think of nothing quite so comforting and so reassuring as to have a delegation from our neighbouring country come to visit us, to whom we can refer with earnestness and in truth and in fact not only as neighbours, Mr. Speaker, but as friends.
It brings a real note of comfort, as with our eyes, as Ishmael did of old, contemplate the horizons of the world and a sea of troubles, to consider how fortunate we are. We hope that you deem yourself equally fortunate that we are your neighbours. It is great comfort that we can live together in amity and concord without troops and without any other visible military evidences, because of the understanding that we have had for such a long time.
As minority leader, I welcome you to the Senate.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext: Mr. President, I merely wish to say to these gentlemen that it is a pleasure for us and a great honor to have you here. We hope that you will come very often.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. President, as a representative of the state of New York, a considerable part of which borders on our great friends to the north, I wish to extend greetings to this distinguished group. I have spent many happy hours in Canada, and I have always enjoyed my visits there. I have many Canadian friends. I am sure that many of you gentlemen have close friends in the United States. My city of Rochester is to a large extent populated by people who were bom in Canada and who cherish their ties to the north. We have very close relations with our Canadian neighbours. The Rochester yacht club sponsors a very spirited contest, as you probably know, with our Canadian friends, in which we have been frequently bested, but we never give up.
I am delighted to note that so many of our guests from the north have elected to sit on this side of the aisle in the Senate. There are a great many vacant chairs here, and we welcome them on this side of the aisle. We congratulate them on their good judgment, and are perfectly delighted to have some of these vacant chairs filled.
I know our friends will not take it amiss when I say that, if we cannot have more Republicans, then there is no one else we would rather have in these chairs, no one else in whose presence we would take greater pride or pleasure than our good friends from the north.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
I too wish to join in extending a friendly and cordial welcome to our fellow parliamentarians from Canada, who are our good friends.

After listening to the lucid comment of my friend from New York, I am reminded of one part of our foreign aid and foreign policy programs, the exchange program. As a member of the Senate on this side of the aisle I would not mind proposing an exchange for some of the regular attendants on that side of the aisle for those I see presently on that side of the aisle. (Laughter)
We welcome you and we want you to know that your presence in the Senate is a source of satisfaction and joy to us.
My state of Minnesota borders on Canada. Many times we have travelled to the great city of Winnipeg. Many of our people make regular journeys over there. Many of your people come to Minnesota.
We are at the other end, so to speak, of the St. Lawrence seaway. We are joined to you not only by the great land mass of the Nort American continent, but also by the great St. Lawrence seaway.
We wish to express our appreciation to our friends from Canada for their leadership in the consummation of this, one of the great public works projects of all time.
Finally, I express my appreciation to them for their leadership in the councils of diplomacy. Canada has demonstrated mature statesmanship, particularly at the United Nations. That leadership has had a very good effect and a very good conditioning upon the deliberations of the United Nations, and we thank you for it. We herald you also for your tremendous economic growth in recent years, and the capacity you have demonstrated of being able to roll with the punches of your economic growth and expansion. We congratulate you upon your prosperity and upon your sharing of the fruits of your production. We also congratulate you upon your population growth. Surely in your great country there is so much room for so many good people.
Frankly, we are happy, as the minority leader said, in these trying days, to have such wonderful good friends, even when you occasionally tell us things that we may not want to hear, even though we may deserve to hear them. We shall reciprocate in kind but in a kindly way.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
It is a wonderful thing in this troubled world to have representatives from another nation come to visit us, particularly to have these visits made by people who believe as we do and work along with us in our efforts to make this a better world. If all the nations of the world believed as you do it would be a much better world to live in. So we are thankful today to have you come to visit us here in the United States, as we face the problems that we are facing, and realize that we have you right to 90205-6-480J
the north of us, and that you are our right hand, so to speak, in helping solve the problems of the world. May you continue to grow and not only prosper materially but also prosper in giving all the people the liberties that belong to them. God bless you and may you continue to grow is the wish of all the senators at this time.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. President, I wish to join my colleague from New York in welcoming the Canadian parliamentarians, and to express on this rare occasion my appreciation for the many long-standing favours conferred upon my state through my person.
When I was attorney general I had the opportunity to co-operate with your authorities in finding and punishing rascals in the security field. I received enormous co-operation from your officials. During the war, as an army officer, I worked with your minister of munitions. In more recent days I had the honour of dining with Prime Minister Diefenbaker and his cabinet, including the late departed and lamented Mr. Smith, a very dear friend of mine, and a wonderful man.
I have also visited and participated in the inauguration of power projects connected with the seaway, and in the Niagara frontier area, where we are working together.
As my tribute, as a senator from the state of New York, to the great Dominion of Canada, a great, stanch, and true friend, as has been so eloquently stated by my colleague, the distinguished junior Senator from New York (Mr. Keating), I may say that we have demonstrated that free peoples can work together in a discipline, nothwithstanding the fact that self interest may often dictate our pulling apart.
In the final analysis, no matter how frank you may be with us-and even critical at times-we all know that, like a couple who are married, this has all got to be lived with until there is a better day or a sunnier side to our relations, because we are indissolubly linked together.
I think it is this deep conviction which we all carry, and which is so particularly true in the States which border on Canada that represents one of the enormous strengths of freedom throughout the world. I do not think any nation in the world, even behind the iron curtain, doubts that Canada and the United States will always stand together, and that any hopes of separating them in any way are bound to be dashed. This is one of the most enormous strengths which freedom has.
I am delighted to welcome you and to speak to you in that spirit.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. President, I have had the honor this morning, in the absence of the

co-chairman of our delegation, the senator from Vermont (Mr. Aiken), to welcome our distinguished visitors to Washington and to the United States. To do this again would be, indeed, surplusage. However, for the Record, I think perhaps it should be said that this particular meeting has been of unique value, a value which is not found in any other type of meeting. That unique value is that members of the House of Representatives and members of the U. S. Senate, and members of the House of Commons and members of the Canadian Senate, are able to meet together and discuss frankly every phase of our relationships-our cultural relationships, our tourist relationships, our economic relationships, our common interest in matters of defence, our common interests in the salvation of freedom throughout the world; and to do this frankly, without any fear of having spoken something which is contrary to the spirit of our respective governments, because none of us can speak for our governments, even though two distinguished Speakers of the parliament of Canada are here.
So if in the days ahead it should be asked what we hope to accomplish by this meeting it may be said we hope to accomplish the great area of understanding which friends seek- and understanding which is based upon giving and taking, and giving and forgiving; an area which we know will lead to more fruitful relationships in every respect between our countries.
The unique value of this meeting is that we meet without fear of doing something which may be taken as binding upon our governments. We meet in a spirit of friendship and frankness, which brings to all of us an education as to the desires and the possibilities of the future. That is something which we need.
Again, I welcome our Canadian friends to Washington and to the United States.

maintopic: VISIT TO THE SENATE BY CANADIAN DELEGATION TO THE CANADA-UNITED STATES INTERPARLIAMENTARY GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. President, I join with other senators in welcoming the members of the Canadian parliament to our hall and to our country. I was a member of the interparliamentary committee which went to Canada in February. We received from the members of the Canadian parliament a most cordial and hospitable welcome, a welcome much unlike, as I told them, the first welcome I received from the Canadian people, when I was deported from Canada in 1929. That incident took place when I was a member of the R.O.T.C. team from the University of Hawaii. We went to Camp Perry, Ohio, and then crossed the Detroit river in an attempt to go to Windsor. At that time the Canadians told me I had to post a bond if I wanted to enter Canada. So I returned to the United States, at the invitation of the Canadian government,
and they paid my transportation fare of five cents across the Detroit river. (Laughter).
Mr. President, the meetings which the interparliamentary committee held in Canada in February were most fruitful. I was much impressed with the earnestness and the seriousness of the views of our neighbours across the border. I know that their problems and our problems can be solved most amicably. I came away from that meeting with a better concept of their problems, knowing that the differences which exist between the United States and Canada are minor compared with the may things which we have in common.
We in this hemisphere have mutual problems, and we know that by discussing them together from time to time, as we did in Canada in February, and now, again, in the United States, we shall be able to solve them.
I look forward to long lasting friendship and amity with the Canadian people. I know that this friendship will endure to all eternity. I thank the representatives of the Canadian parliament for coming to visit us. I know that our deliberations will be fruitful for both the United States and Canada.
Again, I convey my welcome to the Canadian parliamentarians, and am grateful to them for having taken the time to come and visit us.
The Presiding Officer (Mr. Hickey in the Chair): The Chair joins in the hearty welcome accorded by senators to our brethren from our northern neighbour; and trusts that their sojourn in our capital city will prove both pleasant and profitable.

Report of Defence and Foreign Policy Committee
1.	Western Hemisphere Co-operation:
(a) Canadian participation in the O.A.S United States members supported President Kennedy's recent suggestion that Canada consider joining the O.A.S. Canadian members agreed that Canada and the United States must stand together in supporting common objectives within the hemisphere, to raise standards of living and help meet the communist threat. The problem for Canada is to decide whether joining the O.A.S. would be in the best interest of Canada and the western hemisphere. This question is the subject of lively public discussion in Canada at the present time.
Among the arguments advanced in favour of Canada's association with the O.A.S. were the assistance which Canada might be able to give toward raising living standards in Latin America, the additional weight of

Canadian leadership and stability in hemispheric policy discussions, removal of the anomaly of Canadian participation in NATO but not in O.A.S., and removal of doubt about Canada's support of the principles on which O.A.S. is founded.
Among the arguments mentioned in opposition to Canadian participation in O.A.S. were the limitations on Canada's resources, the risk that Canada's position in O.A.S. would either be labeled as that of a satellite of the United States or would be harmful to United States prestige to the extent that Canada's attitudes diverged from that of the United States on significant issues, and finally the loss of Canada's ability to present an uncommitted view on problems arising in the hemisphere.
(b) Cuba: There was complete agreement on the serious threat which communist influence in Cuba presents to the whole hemisphere. With respect to methods of countering this danger, however, there were two basically different approaches. Some felt that the situation warranted drastic measures. Others believed the Cuban revolution was brought about by underlying causes which are to be found in many other areas in Latin America. These unhealthy tendencies must be dealt with on a long term basis through programs of economic assistance, information, cultural interchange, and foreign policies in the interest of the freedom and economic opportunity of mankind. The committee agreed that there is need for expressing to the peoples of less developed countries the social objectives of our society. To compete successfully with the communists in the emerging countries we must explain our system in terms of social justice as well as personal freedom.
2.	Strengthening NATO:
There was full agreement of the necessity of strengthening the conventional forces assigned to NATO. It was noted that both Canada and the United States have met their NATO force goals. Several specific NATO defence problems were discussed: the desirability of having small nuclear weapons for tactical use; the inhibition on the use of major nuclear weapons in the absence of adequate conventional forces; the question of control by a multi-national organization over a NATO nuclear strategic force; and the necessity of making the United States nuclear retaliatory weapons invulnerable. It was recognized that if the Soviet union moved at any time in force to cut off access to West Berlin, NATO would be ready to respond with the necessary force.
3.	China Policy:
The committee discussed trade with communist China. The members were agreed that there should be no trade in strategic goods. The Canadian members, however, stated that in Canada there was general support for a policy of trade with China in nonstrategic goods on the grounds that to cut off all trade would not weaken the hold of the Chinese communist party and that trade helps maintain the strength of the Canadian economy. The view was also expressed that it can assist in some measure to preserve a small reservoir of good will in China which could be of long term benefit to the west. Some United States members, while acknowledging that the United States does trade in certain non-strategic commodities with countries of eastern Europe, were of the view that trade materially assists the Chinese in reaching their economic objectives, raises moral issues on which the United States public feels deeply and strengthens the Chinese position in Asia. The Canadian chairman referred with pleasure to the statement made in the House of Commons the previous day by the Prime Minister regarding the happy solution to the difficulty which had arisen over the supply from United States sources of grain unloading equipment and the committee agreed that this was a good example of continuing co-operation between, the two countries.
The committee also discussed the closely related questions of diplomatic recognition of communist China and its representation in the United Nations. While neither Canada nor the United States has yet recognized the People's Republic of China, it was generally agreed that the issue of representation in the United Nations would soon confront the two nations and that at the forthcoming meeting of the general assembly there would likely be increased support for seating representatives of communist China. The "two China" concept was also considered as a possible solution for the representation of China. It was pointed out that the admission of a Chinese communist delegation to the United Nations would be interpreted in many places in the United States as an act of appeasement and might lead to strong demands that the United States leave the United Nations. The Canadian members pointed out that Canadian public opinion is divided on the issue.
4. Disarmament
The committee agreed that disarmament negotiations must be continued despite the difficulties and lack of concrete progress so
